idiom_name: Predicate<T> / Func<T, bool> + lambdas (LINQ for collections)
implementation_notes: Predicate<T> and Func<T, bool> are the carriers and C# delegates are first-class values, so contramap is a lambda over a projection, divide is x => a(x) && b(x), negate is x => !a(x), and choose is a switch expression over a closed hierarchy or a discriminator field. C# has no higher-kinded types, so there is no typeclass to implement, and a boolean delegate has no reason slot: for user-facing validation the ecosystem answer is a rule builder (FluentValidation) or attribute validation (DataAnnotations) rather than hand-rolled delegates.
pitfalls: Delegate composition allocates a closure per combination and every Func<T, bool> invocation is indirect - fine while the rule set is built once, measurable inside a per-item loop.
Predicate<T> and Func<T, bool> are distinct delegate types with no implicit conversion on older targets, so mixed APIs force adapter lambdas: pick one and stay with it.
Hand-written delegate rules lose translatability: an Expression<Func<T, bool>> can be sent to EF Core or rendered as a message tree, while a composed Func<T, bool> cannot.

variants.name: FluentValidation rule builder (declarative, accumulating)
variants.implementation_notes: FluentValidation replaces the hand-written combinator layer with a DSL: RuleFor(x => x.Email).NotEmpty().EmailAddress() is contramap onto a projection, SetValidator(new InnerValidator()) is divide (nested validators run and their failures accumulate), and When/Unless/Otherwise express conditional dispatch - the closest C# idiom to choose. The result is a ValidationResult holding every failure, which is what forms and APIs need; choose this whenever rules are business-owned, localized, or shared between web and background entry points.
pitfalls: A child validator registered with SetValidator is skipped when the parent property is null (its default cascade), so 'missing' and 'invalid' must be separated by an explicit NotNull() rule.

Validators are instantiated per validation pass and rule conditions are evaluated at validation time: storing per-request state in validator fields is the classic way to leak data between requests - keep them stateless.
